concept: The out-of-pocket max caps what you pay for COVERED, IN-NETWORK care in a plan year. Once you hit it (deductible + coinsurance + qualifying copays), the plan pays 100% the rest of the year. It does NOT include your monthly premiums, out-of-network balance billing, or services your plan doesn't cover at all. So 'OOP max' is your worst case within the plan's rules — not necessarily your worst total spend if something falls outside them.
shortcut: After deductible, pay coinsurance until you hit the OOP max. On a $50,000 in-network hospital stay with $2,000 deductible and $6,000 OOP max: you pay at most $6,000 for that care; insurance covers the rest. Add 12 × premium to get your real annual outlay in a max-use year.
example:
In-network hospital bill: $50,000
Deductible: $2,000
Coinsurance: 20%
OOP max: $6,000
You pay for that care: $6,000 (capped)
Insurance: $44,000

Not counted: premiums ($300/mo × 12 = $3,600), any out-of-network charges, non-covered services.

title: HDHP vs PPO comparison
concept: A High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) has lower premiums but higher deductibles. A PPO has higher premiums but lower out-of-pocket costs. HDHPs make sense if you're healthy and rarely use healthcare. PPOs win if you have regular medical needs or expect major procedures.
shortcut: HDHP total = lower premium × 12 + higher deductible. PPO total = higher premium × 12 + lower deductible. If HDHP worst-case < PPO worst-case, HDHP saves money. Also: HDHPs qualify for HSAs.
example:
HDHP: $200/mo, $3,000 deductible
Worst case: $5,400

PPO: $400/mo, $500 deductible
Worst case: $5,300

PPO wins by $100 in worst case
but HDHP saves $2,400 if healthy

title: HSA triple tax advantage
concept: HSAs have the triple tax advantage: contributions are pre-tax (reduce taxable income AND payroll tax if via Section 125), growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical are tax-free at any age. The hidden superpower: after age 65, you can withdraw HSA funds for ANY purpose (just pay ordinary income tax, like a Traditional IRA). 2025 contribution limits: $4,300 self-only / $8,550 family (per IRS Rev Proc 2024-25). You must be enrolled in a qualifying HDHP (2025 minimum deductible: $1,650 self / $3,300 family) to contribute. This combination makes the HSA arguably the most tax-efficient retirement account in the US code.
shortcut: Annual tax saving = contribution × (your income tax rate + ~7.65% FICA if contributed via payroll). Long-term: HSA grows like an investment account. $3,500/yr from age 30 to 65 at 7% growth ≈ $550,000, all tax-free for medical or income-taxed for anything else.
example:
Contribute $3,000 at 22% rate via payroll:
Income tax saved: $660
FICA saved (7.65%): $230
Total immediate saving: $890

Long-term:
$3,500/yr × 35 yrs at 7% growth
≈ $550,000
Used for medical: $0 tax
Used for retirement (after 65): ordinary income tax only

title: FSA: free money or wasted money?
concept: Flexible Spending Accounts are use-it-or-lose-it: any unspent balance at year-end is generally forfeited. Employers can offer one (not both) of two grace mechanisms: a 2.5-month grace period to spend prior-year funds, or a limited rollover (IRS-indexed; ~$660 for 2025 per IRS Rev Proc). 2025 contribution cap: $3,300 per employee (per IRS). Tax savings = election × your tax rate. If you elect $3,000 at a 25% bracket, you save $750 in tax. But if you only spend $1,800, you forfeit $1,200 — for a net loss of $450.
shortcut: Only elect what you'll definitely spend. Tax savings = election × tax rate. Break-even: spend at least (1 − tax rate) of your election. In a 25% bracket, you need to spend at least 75% of what you elect to come out ahead.
example:
Election: $2,850 at 25% bracket
Tax savings: $712

Scenario A: Spend $2,850 → save $712 ✓
Scenario B: Spend $1,800 → save $712 in tax but lose $1,050 unused
Net: −$338

title: How much life insurance do you actually need?
concept: Two methods: (1) The 10-12× rule of thumb — multiply annual income by 10. (2) DIME method: Debt + Income replacement + Mortgage + Education costs. Add mortgage balance, subtract savings/existing coverage. Term life (20-30 years) is what most young families need — way cheaper than whole life.
shortcut: Quick estimate: salary × 10 = baseline coverage. Adjusted: + mortgage − savings. Compare two quotes by the annual cost per $100k of coverage.
example:
Salary: $70,000
10× rule: $700,000 baseline
Mortgage: +$280,000
Savings: −$50,000
Adjusted: $930,000 needed

Term quotes (30yr, healthy 35yo):
$500k @ $35/mo = $420/yr
$1M @ $55/mo = $660/yr

title: Brand name vs generic — the prescription math
concept: Generic drugs are chemically identical to brand-name versions but cost 80-85% less. With 12 monthly refills, a $35 copay difference becomes $420/year. When your doctor prescribes a brand-name drug, always ask if there's a generic.
shortcut: Annual saving per prescription = (brand copay − generic copay) × 12. For multiple prescriptions, sum the differences. Sometimes GoodRx cash price for generics is cheaper than insurance brand copay.
example:
Brand copay: $45
Generic copay: $10
Monthly diff: $35
Annual saving: $420

Two prescriptions switched to generic:
($35 + $20) × 12 = $660/year saved

title: What insurance policies do you actually need?
concept: Most adults are over-insured on some policies (extended warranties, pet insurance) and under-insured on others (disability, umbrella liability). The priority order: health > auto/renter's-or-home > life (with dependents) > disability > umbrella > pet > extended warranty. The principle: SELF-INSURE small risks (extended warranties, low deductibles), TRANSFER catastrophic ones (health, disability, liability).
shortcut: Rule: insure against what would be financially ruinous, NOT against minor inconveniences. A broken phone is annoying ($800). A hospital stay or year of disability is ruinous ($50k-$500k). Skip extended warranties, raise your auto deductible, but max out health and consider disability.
example:
Priority order (essential to optional):
1. Health insurance       — catastrophic protection
2. Auto + renter's/home   — required + liability
3. Life (if dependents)   — replace your income
4. Disability             — far more likely than death
5. Umbrella liability     — once net worth > $500k
6. Pet insurance          — optional
7. Extended warranties    — almost never worth it

title: Disability insurance — the one no one talks about
concept: You're statistically far more likely to be disabled than to die during your working years. The Social Security Administration estimates about 1 in 4 of today's 20-year-olds will become disabled before reaching retirement age (per SSA Disability Basic Facts). Yet most workers carry only basic employer-provided long-term disability — typically 60% of base salary, capped, and on an 'any-occupation' definition (no payout if you can do ANY job, even minimum-wage).
shortcut: Three things to check on your disability coverage: (1) own-occupation vs any-occupation (own-occ pays if you can't do YOUR specific job — much better, much pricier), (2) coverage cap (employer LTD caps low for high earners), (3) elimination period (the waiting period before benefits start — typically 90 days, so you need an emergency fund to bridge that gap).
example:
Why disability > life insurance for most working-age adults (per SSA):
Probability before age 65:
  Disability 90+ days: ~25%
  Death: ~5-7%

Employer LTD limits hurt high earners:
  Salary $200k, LTD pays 60% = $120k
  Capped at $10k/month = $120k/yr cap
  Above $200k earners may need supplemental private coverage.

title: Open enrollment — the 10-minute checklist
concept: Open enrollment is the ~2-week window each fall (typically Oct-Nov for a plan year starting Jan 1) when you pick all your employer benefits for the next 12 months. Miss it and you're locked in until next year unless you have a qualifying life event (marriage, baby, divorce, job loss). The mistake most people make: re-electing the same things from last year on autopilot. The 10-minute checklist that beats most people's outcomes: (1) **Medical plan** — HDHP vs PPO based on EXPECTED use this year (low: HDHP wins on premium; high: PPO wins on OOP). (2) **HSA or FSA** — HSA only if HDHP enrolled, $4,300 self / $8,550 family 2025 cap (per IRS Rev Proc 2024-25); FSA $3,300/yr 2025 cap (per IRS), use-it-or-lose-it. (3) **Dependent Care FSA** — $5,000/yr cap (per IRS, not inflation-indexed), pre-tax for daycare / aftercare. (4) **Commuter benefits** — $315/mo each for transit + parking (2025, per IRS), pre-tax. (5) **Life insurance** — most employers give 1× salary free; supplemental usually 2-5× pre-tax. (6) **Disability** — confirm short-term and long-term coverage; check 'own-occupation' vs 'any-occupation' definitions. (7) **401(k) contribution rate** — open enrollment is also a good moment to bump.
shortcut: Four-stage rule: **estimate your medical year** (low / medium / high use) → **pick HDHP or PPO** accordingly → **fund the right account** (HSA with HDHP, or FSA with PPO) → **review supplemental** (DCFSA if you have kids, commuter if you commute, supplemental life only if you actually have dependents). Skip: most accident / hospital-indemnity / cancer-only / legal / identity-theft add-ons sold during open enrollment — they're usually negative expected value. Confirm: your 401(k) rate is at LEAST the employer match cap.
example:
Decision flow for a typical 30-something:

Single, healthy, no kids, low medical use:
  Medical: HDHP (lowest premium, low OOP risk)
  HSA: max out ($4,300 self, 2025) — triple tax advantage
  FSA: skip (HDHPs and Health FSAs don't combine; limited-purpose FSA allowed)
  DCFSA: skip (no dependents)
  Commuter: yes if commuting
  Supplemental life: skip (no dependents)
  Supplemental disability: maybe (cheap pre-tax via employer)
  Estimated annual tax saving: ~$1,200-1,800 from HSA alone at 22-24% bracket

Married with infant in daycare:
  Medical: PPO (kids = high medical-use risk)
  HSA: not available (PPO usually not HSA-eligible)
  FSA: $3,300 (2025) for predictable medical / dental / vision
  DCFSA: $5,000 (2025) for daycare — typically the highest-ROI election
  Commuter: yes
  Supplemental life: 2-5× salary (dependent income replacement)
  Estimated annual tax saving: ~$1,500-2,200 (FSA + DCFSA + commuter combined)

The 10-minute pass beats 90% of 'I just re-elected last year's plan' outcomes — most people leave $500-1,500/yr of tax savings on the table by skipping the DCFSA or commuter election.

title: Monthly payment vs total cost
concept: Dealers love to talk monthly payments because they sound affordable. But total cost = monthly payment × number of months. A $450/month payment over 72 months means you're paying $32,400 total. Always calculate the full cost before signing.
shortcut: Total cost = payment × months. Interest paid = total cost − loan amount. A $25,000 car at $450/month for 72 months costs $32,400 — that's $7,400 in interest.
example:
Loan: $25,000
Payment: $450/month × 72 months
Total: $32,400
Interest: $7,400

title: The hidden cost of '24 more months'
concept: Salespeople love long loan terms because they lower the monthly payment — and increase total interest. Extending from 48 to 72 months can drop your payment $130/month but add $3,800+ in total cost. Focus on the delta between terms, not the headline payment.
shortcut: Total cost difference = (payment_longer × months_longer) − (payment_shorter × months_shorter). Lower payment ≠ better deal. The extra months are pure interest extraction.
example:
Same $25,000 loan:
48 months × $550 = $26,400
72 months × $420 = $30,240
Extra cost of longer term: $3,840

Monthly 'savings' from 48→72: $130
Total cost increase: $3,840
The trade-off is bad.

title: Down payment math
concept: A down payment doesn't just reduce what you borrow — it eliminates interest on that money. On a 5-year loan at 7%, a $5k down payment saves $5k principal + ~$900 interest = $5,900 in total cost. But there's an opportunity cost: that $5k could've been invested. The math: if your loan rate (after tax) is HIGHER than your expected investment return, down payment wins. At 7% car loan vs 8% stock returns, it's almost a wash — invest if you have other high-rate debt, down-payment if you don't.
shortcut: Down payment = price × down%. Loan = price − down. Interest saved by larger down ≈ extra down × loan rate × term/2. But: opportunity cost. $5k invested at 8% becomes ~$7,300 in 5 years. If your loan rate > expected investment return, down-pay. Otherwise consider investing the extra cash instead.
example:
$30,000 car, 7% APR, 60 months:
0% down: $5,700 interest
20% down ($6,000): borrow $24k, $4,560 interest
Difference: $1,140 interest saved

Opportunity cost check:
$6,000 invested at 8% × 5 yrs ≈ $8,800 (gain $2,800)
Down payment saves $1,140; investing earns $2,800.
If you have no other high-rate debt, the math favors investing the $6k and taking the smaller down.

title: The 20/4/10 rule
concept: Financial experts recommend: 20% down payment, 4-year (48-month) max loan term, and total car costs under 10% of gross monthly income. This rule keeps you from being 'car poor' — spending so much on your car that it squeezes everything else.
shortcut: Max car cost (10% rule) = monthly gross income × 10%. That includes payment + insurance + gas. If you earn $5,000/month gross, max total car costs = $500/month.
example:
Monthly income: $5,000
10% max car cost: $500/month
Includes: payment + insurance + gas
If insurance + gas = $200
Max payment: $300/month

title: Car depreciation math
concept: New cars lose about 20% of their value in the first year and roughly 15% per year after that. A $35,000 car is worth about $28,000 after year one. Understanding depreciation helps you decide between new, certified pre-owned, and used.
shortcut: Value after year 1 = price × 80%. Value after year 2 ≈ year 1 value × 85%. Quick estimate: a car loses about half its value in 3-4 years.
example:
New car: $35,000
After year 1 (−20%): $28,000
After year 2 (−15%): $23,800
Lost $11,200 in 2 years

title: What your car really costs per month
concept: Monthly car cost ≠ monthly payment. The real number includes payment + insurance + gas + maintenance + depreciation. For most cars, that's $300-$400/month ON TOP of the payment. A $400 payment becomes a $700-$800/month total cost.
shortcut: Add payment + ~$150 insurance + ~$150 gas + ~$80 maintenance as baseline non-payment costs. Total monthly ownership = payment + $380 (typical). Add depreciation if you're tracking true cost.
example:
Payment: $400
Insurance: $150
Gas: $200
Maintenance: $80
Total monthly cost: $830

Reality: $830 × 12 = $9,960/year of car expenses, not $4,800.

title: Lease vs buy — the 3-year math
concept: Leasing: $350/month × 36 months = $12,600 spent, you own nothing at the end. Buying: $500/month × 60 months = $30,000, but after 36 months the car is worth ~$20,000. Your net 'cost' after 36 months: $30k payments − $20k value = $10k net. For the same 3 years, leasing cost you $2,600 more AND you have nothing to sell.
shortcut: Lease cost over term = monthly × months. Buy net cost over same term = (monthly × months) − resale value. Lower number wins. Buying almost always cheaper if you keep the car past the loan.
example:
Compare 3 years:
LEASE: $350 × 36 = $12,600 spent (own nothing)
BUY: $500 × 36 = $18,000 paid, car worth $20,000
Net: $18k − $20k = −$2,000 (you BUILT $2k equity)
Buying wins by $14,600 over 3 years

title: Is the dealer trade-in rip-off worth it?
concept: Dealers offer convenience but lowball trade-in prices. The spread between trade-in and private sale is typically $2,000-$4,000. Private selling takes time (2-4 weeks of effort) but the difference often comes out to $100-$200/hour of effort. Tax wrinkle: in most states, trading in reduces your sales tax base on the new car.
shortcut: Trade-in premium = private sale price − trade-in offer. Effective hourly = premium ÷ estimated hours of selling effort. Tax benefit of trade-in = (trade-in value) × your state sales tax rate.
example:
Car: $11,000 private market, $8,000 trade-in offer
Premium: $3,000
Estimated hours: 20 (photos, listings, calls, test drives, paperwork)
Effective: $150/hour

Tax benefit (trade-in): $8,000 × 8% = $640 less sales tax
Adjusted premium: $3,000 − $640 = $2,360

title: Dealer tactics — what to watch for
concept: Car dealerships have refined their tactics over decades. The 'four-square' worksheet that combines trade-in, down payment, monthly payment, and price into one confusing grid (designed to hide markup). The 'what payment can you afford?' trap (extends the term to inflate your total cost). The F&I (Finance & Insurance) office where they pitch GAP insurance, paint protection, and extended warranties at markup. Financing markup (dealers add 1-3% to the rate the lender quoted them). Document fees (often $300-$700, sometimes negotiable).
shortcut: Negotiate ONE number: out-the-door price. Refuse to discuss monthly payment or trade-in until OTD is locked. Get pre-approved financing from your bank BEFORE walking in. Decline everything in the F&I office (extended warranty, GAP, paint protection) — you can buy these elsewhere for half the price.
example:
The 'monthly payment' trap:
$30,000 car at $500/mo for 60 months = $30,000 paid (0% interest example, ignore)
But $30,000 car at $500/mo for 72 months = $36,000 paid
Same monthly comfort, $6,000 more paid

Dealer F&I markup example:
Lender quotes 6% APR to dealer
Dealer offers you 7.5%
On $25k loan over 5 years: $1,000+ in extra interest, paid as F&I commission

title: Manufacturer vs extended warranty
concept: Most new cars come with a manufacturer warranty: typically 3 years / 36,000 miles bumper-to-bumper, 5 years / 60,000 miles powertrain (varies by automaker — Hyundai/Kia and Mitsubishi offer 10-year powertrain). Extended warranties / service contracts (sold by the dealer F&I office) add 1-7 years for $1,000-$3,000. Consumer Reports surveys of car owners consistently find the majority never use their extended warranty, and those who do recoup less than what they paid on average (per Consumer Reports auto reliability surveys). The expected value is negative — it's insurance against repair anxiety, not a financial product.
shortcut: Pass on extended warranties for: reliable brands (Toyota, Honda, Lexus — per Consumer Reports reliability rankings), cars you'll sell before warranty expires, anyone who can self-insure (save $30/month for repairs instead). Consider extended warranties only for: first-year electric vehicles (high parts cost, less proven), or luxury European brands with notoriously expensive repairs (BMW, Mercedes, Audi, Land Rover).
example:
Extended warranty math:
Cost: $2,000 for 5 extra years
Avg payout (per CR surveys): well under $2k for most buyers
Expected loss: typically several hundred dollars

Alternative: self-insure
Save $33/month → $2,000 by year 5
If no major repair: you keep $2,000
If major repair ($1,500): still net positive $500

title: Student loan monthly payment
concept: Standard 10-year repayment costs about $100-$120 per $10,000 borrowed at typical 4-7% rates. A $30k loan ≈ $300-$360/month. A $50k loan ≈ $500-$600/month. This rule is accurate within 10% of the actual amortized payment.
shortcut: Per $10k borrowed at 4-7% APR over 10 years: ~$100-$120/month. Higher rate = closer to $120. Quick mental math: divide your balance by $10k, multiply by your per-$10k rate.
example:
Loan $40,000:
$40k ÷ $10k = 4
× $110 (~5% APR) = $440/month

Loan $25,000 at 6%:
2.5 × $115 = ~$287/month
Actual amortized: $278 (within $10)

title: Total cost of student loans
concept: Total repayment = monthly payment × number of months. Subtract the original loan to find total interest. A 10-year loan at 5-6% typically costs ~25-30% of original balance in interest. $40k loan? Expect $10k-$12k extra in interest.
shortcut: Total cost = payment × months. Interest = total − loan. Interest as % = interest ÷ loan × 100. Quick benchmark: 10-yr loan at 5-6% = ~28% interest premium.
example:
$30,000 loan, $318/mo × 120 months:
Total: $38,160
Interest: $8,160
Interest %: 27.2%

Within the 25-30% benchmark for standard repayment.

title: Refinancing savings
concept: Refinancing replaces your current loan with a new one at a lower interest rate. The savings come from the rate difference applied to your balance. Dropping from 6% to 4% on a $40,000 balance saves roughly $800/year in interest.
shortcut: Annual interest saving ≈ balance × (old rate − new rate). $40,000 × (6% − 4%) = $800/year. Over 10 years, that's $8,000 in savings — but you lose federal loan protections.
example:
Balance: $40,000
Old rate: 6%, New rate: 4%
Annual saving: $40,000 × 2% = $800
10-year saving: ~$8,000

title: Income-driven repayment
concept: Income-driven repayment (IDR) caps federal student-loan payments at a percentage of your 'discretionary income' (income above a poverty-line multiplier). Different plans — SAVE, PAYE, IBR, ICR — use different formulas, family-size adjustments, and forgiveness timelines (20-25 years). After 2024-25 court rulings vacated parts of SAVE, the rules and plan availability are in active flux. Only federal Direct Loans qualify; private loans don't. Always check current Federal Student Aid plan terms before committing.
shortcut: Mental baseline (pre-SAVE canonical formula): monthly ≈ (income − 1.5 × poverty line) × 10% ÷ 12. Use this for rough sanity-checks only — your actual payment depends on the specific plan (formulas vary 5%-20%), your family size, and current federal rules. Confirm on the FSA Loan Simulator before any decision.
example:
Baseline illustration (canonical 10%/150% formula):
Income: $50,000
Poverty line × 1.5: $22,500
Discretionary: $27,500
Monthly ≈ $27,500 × 10% ÷ 12 ≈ $229

Real-world: your actual IDR plan, family size, and current SAVE-era rules can move this materially. Use as a directional check, not a quote.

title: PSLF forgiveness math
concept: Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) forgives remaining federal loan balance after 120 qualifying payments (10 years) while working for a qualifying employer. The key math: total paid = IDR payment × 120 months. Forgiven amount = original balance + accrued interest − total paid.
shortcut: PSLF total paid = monthly IDR payment × 120. Forgiveness amount = remaining balance at month 120. If you pay $250/month for 10 years = $30,000 paid. If balance started at $80,000, you could get $50,000+ forgiven.
example:
Loan: $80,000
IDR payment: $250/month
10 years = $30,000 paid
Forgiven: $50,000+
(balance grew with interest)

title: Does your employer pay your student loans?
concept: If your employer offers it, IRC § 127 lets them contribute up to $5,250/year tax-free toward your student loans — made permanent under the OBBBA in 2025. Adoption is still uncommon: around 26% of employers offered it in 2024 (per SHRM 2024 Employee Benefits Survey), heavily skewed toward larger employers, professional services, healthcare, and tech. So this isn't a default benefit to assume — but if your benefits package includes it, it's effectively a $437.50/month tax-free raise that goes straight to principal.
shortcut: Annual benefit ÷ 12 = monthly principal contribution. Multi-year value: benefit × years + interest you avoid (rough: benefit × your rate × half the remaining years, because the principal shrinks linearly). Check your benefits portal for 'student loan repayment' or 'education assistance' line items — it's often filed under the wrong header.
example:
Your employer offers the max $5,250/yr (per IRC § 127):
Monthly: $437.50 straight to principal

5 years of full benefit:
$26,250 paid by employer
+ ~$2,000 in interest you avoid (on a 6% loan)
Total value: ~$28,250 — equivalent to a $5,650/yr tax-free raise.

title: Your loans are growing while you wait
concept: Unsubsidized federal loans accrue interest from disbursement. The 6-month grace period after graduation doesn't pause interest — it lets it pile up and capitalize (added to principal). A $25,000 loan at 5.5% accrues ~$680 in interest during grace alone. Most new grads don't realize this.
shortcut: Daily interest = balance × rate ÷ 365. Grace period total = daily × 180 days. Making interest-only payments during grace prevents capitalization and saves money long-term.
example:
$25,000 unsubsidized at 5.5%:
Daily interest: $3.77
Grace period (180 days): $678
New balance at repayment start: $25,678

Interest-only during grace ($113/mo):
Balance stays $25,000 → save $678 + future interest on it

title: Parent PLUS vs private — which costs less?
concept: Parent PLUS loans carry an 8.94% fixed rate (2025-26 academic year) + a 4.228% origination fee deducted upfront. Private parent loans start as low as 5.09% with no origination. For a parent with good credit, private can save $10k+ over 10 years on a $30k loan. But PLUS offers federal protections (IDR, deferment, PSLF) that private doesn't. Rates reset annually each July based on the May Treasury auction.
shortcut: Annual interest difference = balance × (PLUS rate − private rate). Over 10 years × 10. Origination fee adds to PLUS cost upfront. Trade-off: ~$10k savings on private vs federal protections.
example:
$30,000 borrowed:
PLUS at 8.94%: ~$2,682/yr interest + $1,268 origination upfront
Private at 5.5%: ~$1,650/yr interest, no fee

Annual diff: ~$1,032
10-year diff: ~$10,320 + $1,268 = $11,588 saved with private

title: Subsidized vs unsubsidized loans
concept: Subsidized loans are need-based and capped — undergrads with demonstrated financial need on their FAFSA may qualify, up to annual limits ($3,500-$5,500/year per Federal Student Aid). On a subsidized loan, the government pays the interest while you're in school, during the 6-month grace period, and during qualified deferment. Unsubsidized loans are available to all eligible students but accrue interest from disbursement onward. Most graduate loans and Parent PLUS are unsubsidized. The difference compounds: a $25k subsidized loan stays at $25k through graduation; a $25k unsubsidized loan grows to ~$28k over four years at 5.5%.
shortcut: Borrowing order if you have a mix offered: subsidized first (free money on the interest), unsubsidized second, federal Parent PLUS third (worst rate + origination), private last (no federal protections). Don't decline offered subsidized aid because the amount is small — every dollar that doesn't accrue interest in school is worth more than a dollar of unsubsidized borrowing.
example:
$25,000 borrowed, 4 years in school + 6 months grace, 5.5% interest:
Subsidized: balance at repayment start = $25,000
Unsubsidized: balance at repayment start ≈ $31,000

Difference: $6,000 added to principal you'll then pay 5.5% on for 10 more years — another ~$5,000 in lifetime interest.

title: Federal loan protections you lose by refinancing
concept: Refinance salespeople pitch lower rates without mentioning what you give up. Refinancing federal loans to private permanently forfeits: IDR plans (payment based on income), PSLF (forgiveness after 10 years in public service), federal forbearance (pause payments during hardship), death/disability discharge (federal loans wiped if you die or become totally disabled), and any future federal relief (like the COVID-era pause). You CANNOT refi back to federal once you've gone private — it's a one-way door.
shortcut: Refi makes sense only if ALL apply: (1) stable high income, (2) no chance of public-service work, (3) no realistic risk of needing IDR or a hardship pause, (4) you can save 2%+ on rate. For most public-service workers (teachers, non-profit nurses, government employees, public defenders), refi almost never makes sense — the PSLF math alone usually beats any rate savings. If you're not sure about your career trajectory, keep federal until you are.
example:
Refi tradeoff example:
Federal loan: $40k at 6%, 10-year repayment, $444/mo
Private refi: $40k at 4.5%, 10-year repayment, $415/mo
Savings: $29/month = $3,480 over 10 years

What you give up:
— PSLF (could be $20k-$80k forgiven if you'd qualify)
— IDR (payments could drop dramatically if you lose your job)
— COVID-era pause (saved typical borrower $5k-$10k)
Verdict: only worth it if you're confident none of those protections matter for you.
